claims.text: Severe plastic deformation can produce bulk ultrafine-grained or nanocrystalline steels.
Formation of an ultrafine-grained structure by severe plastic deformation generally improves the corrosion resistance of stainless steels relative to coarse-grained material.
Ultrafine-grained stainless steels have greater grain-boundary density than coarse-grained stainless steels.
The increased grain-boundary density accelerates chromium diffusion toward the steel surface.
Ultrafine-grained or nanocrystalline stainless steels develop greater chromium enrichment in their passivation films than coarse-grained stainless steels.
Chromium enrichment of the passivation film in ultrafine-grained stainless steel has been observed by XPS and corrected STEM.
The ultrafine-grained structure promotes selective chromium oxidation.
Grain-boundary-mediated chromium diffusion is the governing cause of selective chromium oxidation and chromium enrichment.
The chromium-enriched passive film is more spatially uniform in ultrafine-grained steel.
A chromium-rich passive layer inhibits propagation of localized corrosion sites.
A chromium-rich passive layer reduces galvanic coupling between microstructural heterogeneities.
Ultrafine-grained samples will have lower corrosion current density than composition-matched coarse-grained samples under identical exposure conditions.
Ultrafine-grained samples will exhibit less pitting and localized corrosion than composition-matched coarse-grained samples.
The proposed comparison keeps alloy composition and exposure conditions constant while varying grain structure.
The mechanism applies only where the steel contains sufficient chromium for passivation to control corrosion behavior.
The grain-refinement effect may become less important under highly reducing conditions or extreme irradiation.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant corrosion-current reduction, chromium enrichment, or reduction in localized attack would falsify the proposed primary mechanism.
